title: King Charles Meets a Cricket Team That Can't Play for Its Own Country
summary: Imagine loving a sport so much, but your country's leaders say you can't play just because you're a girl. That's what happened to the Afghan women's cricket team. The Taliban, who rule Afghanistan, banned women from playing sports. So the team had to escape and now lives in other countries, mostly Australia. But they still play cricket—and they just met King Charles! The King welcomed them at Clarence House in London on a super hot day. He told them, "I'm so glad that you can pursue what you want to do." Player Ekil Latifi left Afghanistan in 2021 when she was 17. She hasn't seen her family in five years. She said the team represents all the women back home who aren't allowed to play. "It's all about the Afghan women back in our country," she said. The team can't play in the Women's T20 World Cup this summer, which is being held in England. That makes them sad, but meeting the King was a big moment. He even joked, "If you lose, you can blame me for interrupting your training." The players gave him a signed shirt and pinned a badge on his suit. Latifi asked the King to say a "posh word" for her. The King also asked if they faced protests as female cricketers in Afghanistan. The team hopes their story will inspire girls everywhere to never give up on their dreams.
why_it_matters: This story reminds us that even when rules seem unfair, people can find ways to keep doing what they love and speak up for others, no matter where they live.

background_read: Afghanistan is a country in Asia. In 2021, a group called the Taliban took over and banned women from playing sports.
King Charles III became the King of the United Kingdom in 2022; he lives in Clarence House, a royal building in London.
The Women's T20 World Cup is a cricket tournament where teams from different countries compete; Afghanistan's women's team cannot play because their home country does not recognize them.
Article_Structure: WHO: The Afghan women's cricket team (now living in Australia) and King Charles III.
WHAT: The team, forced to leave Afghanistan because the Taliban banned women's sports, met the King in London to share their story.
WHY: To show that even without a country to play for, they represent Afghan women who cannot play, and to inspire girls worldwide to keep their dreams alive.

perspectives.description: They feel proud to represent the women of Afghanistan and hope their bravery will someday change the rules. Meeting the King made them feel seen and respected.
They believe women should not play sports or appear in public this way, which is why they banned the team. Many people around the world think this is deeply unfair.
By welcoming the team, the King and others show they stand with women's rights. They believe girls everywhere should be able to follow their passions without fear.
